content.heading: 8.5 Polytopes
content.paragraph: This section studies geometric properties of an important class of compact convex sets called polytopes. These sets arise in all sorts of applications, including game theory, linear programming, and more general optimization problems, such as the design of feedback controls for engineering systems.

A polytope in $\text{ℝ}^{n}$ is the convex hull of a finite set of points. In $\text{ℝ}^{2}$, a polytope is simply a polygon. In $\text{ℝ}^{3}$, a polytope is called a polyhedron. Important features of a polyhedron are its faces, edges, and vertices. For example, the cube has $6$ square faces, $12$ edges, and $8$ vertices. The following definitions provide terminology for higher dimensions as well as $\text{ℝ}^{2}$ and $\text{ℝ}^{3}$. Recall that the dimension of a set in $\text{ℝ}^{n}$ is the dimension of the smallest flat that contains it. Also, note that a polytope is a special type of compact convex set, because a finite set in $\text{ℝ}^{n}$ is compact and the convex hull of this set is compact, by the theorem in the topology terms and facts box in Section 8.4.

note.title: Definition
note.heading: Definition
note.paragraph: Let $S$ be a compact convex subset of $\text{ℝ}^{n}$. A nonempty subset $F$ of $S$ is called a (proper) face of $S$ if $F \neq S$ and there exists a hyperplane $H = \lbrack f:d\rbrack$ such that $F = S \cap H$ and either $f(S) \leq d$ or $f(S) \geq d.$ The hyperplane $H$ is called a supporting hyperplane to $S$. If the dimension of $F$ is $k$, then $F$ is called a $\textit{\textbf{k}}\textbf{-face}$ of $S$.﻿

If $P$ is a polytope of dimension $k$, then $P$ is called a k-polytope. A $\text{0-face}$ of $P$ is called a vertex (plural: vertices), a $\text{1-face}$ is an edge, and a $(k - 1)$-dimensional face is a facet of $S$.﻿

example.heading: Example 1
example.paragraph: Suppose $S$ is a cube in $\text{ℝ}^{3}$. When a plane $H$ is translated through $\text{ℝ}^{3}$ until it just touches (supports) the cube but does not cut through the interior of the cube, there are three possibilities for $H \cap S$, depending on the orientation of $H$. (See Figure 1.)

content.paragraph: Most applications of polytopes involve the vertices in some way, because they have a special property that is identified in the following definition.

note.title: ﻿Definition
note.heading: ﻿Definition
note.paragraph: Let $S$ be a convex set. A point $\textbf{p}$ in $S$ is called an extreme point of $S$ if $\textbf{p}$ is not in the interior of any line segment that lies in $S$. More precisely, if $\textbf{x}$, $\textbf{y} \in S$ and $\textbf{p} \in \overset{‾}{\textbf{xy}}$, then $\textbf{p} = \textbf{x}$ or $\textbf{p} = \textbf{y}$. The set of all extreme points of $S$ is called the profile of $S$.﻿

content.paragraph: A vertex of any compact convex set $S$ is automatically an extreme point of $S$. This fact is proved during the proof of Theorem 14. In working with a polytope, say $P = \text{conv}\{\textbf{v}_{1},\ldots,\textbf{v}_{k}\}$ for $\textbf{v}_{1},\ldots,\textbf{v}_{k}$ in $\text{ℝ}^{n}$, it is usually helpful to know that $\textbf{v}_{1},\ldots,\textbf{v}_{k}$ are the extreme points of $P$. However, such a list might contain extraneous points. For example, some vector $\textbf{v}_{i}$ could be the midpoint of an edge of the polytope. Of course, in this case $\textbf{v}_{i}$ is not really needed to generate the convex hull. The following definition describes the property of the vertices that will make them all extreme points.

note.title: ﻿Definition
note.heading: ﻿Definition
note.paragraph: The set $\{\textbf{v}_{1},\ldots,\textbf{v}_{k}\}$ is a minimal representation of the polytope $P$ if $P = \text{conv}\{\textbf{v}_{1},\ldots,\textbf{v}_{k}\}$ and for each $i = 1,\ldots,k$, $\mathbf{v}_{i} \notin \text{conv\{}\mathbf{v}_{j}:j \neq i\text{\}}$.﻿

content.paragraph: Every polytope has a minimal representation. For if $P = \text{conv}\{\textbf{v}_{1},\ldots,\textbf{v}_{k}\}$ and if some $\textbf{v}_{i}$ is a convex combination of the other points, then $\textbf{v}_{i}$ may be deleted from the set of points without changing the convex hull. This process may be repeated until the minimal representation is left. It can be shown that the minimal representation is unique.

note.title: Theorem ﻿14﻿
note.heading: Theorem ﻿14﻿
note.paragraph: Suppose $M = \{\textbf{v}_{1},\ldots,\textbf{v}_{k}\}$ is the minimal representation of the polytope $P$. Then the following three statements are equivalent:

list.item: p∈M.﻿
p is a vertex of P.﻿
p is an extreme point of P.﻿

content.heading: Proof
content.paragraph: (a) $\Rightarrow$ (b) Suppose $\textbf{p} \in M$ and let $Q = \text{conv}\{\textbf{v}:\textbf{v} \in M$ and $\left. \textbf{v} \neq \textbf{p} \right\}$. It follows from the definition of $M$ that $\textbf{p~}\text{∉}\textbf{~}Q$, and since $Q$ is compact, Theorem 13 implies the existence of a hyperplane $H\prime$ that strictly separates $\{\textbf{p}\}$ and $Q$. Let $H$ be the hyperplane through $\textbf{p}$ parallel to $H\prime$. See Figure 2.

image.alt: A figure shows two parallel vertical lines labeled H and H prime along with a shaded pentagon Q. The line H has a point labeled p at the midpoint. A shaded pentagon Q is seen next to the line H prime with its base facing the line.

content.paragraph: Then $Q$ lies in one of the closed half-spaces $H^{+}$ bounded by $H$ and so $P \subseteq H^{+}$. Thus $H$ supports $P$ at $\textbf{p}$. Furthermore, $\textbf{p}$ is the only point of $P$ that can lie on $H\text{,}$ so $H \cap P = \{\textbf{p}\}$ and $\textbf{p}$ is a vertex of $P$.﻿

(b) $\Rightarrow$ (c) Let $\textbf{p}$ be a vertex of $\textbf{p}$. Then there exists a hyperplane $H = \lbrack f:d\rbrack$ such that $H \cap P = \{\textbf{p}\}$ and $f(P) \geq d$. If $\textbf{p}$ were not an extreme point, then there would exist distinct points $\textbf{x}$ and $\textbf{y}$ in $P$ such that $\textbf{p} = (1 - c)\textbf{x} + c\textbf{y}$ with $0 < c < 1$. That is,

paragraph.math: $$(1 - c)\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{p} - c\mathbf{y}~\text{and~}(1 - c)f\left( \mathbf{x} \right) = d - cf\left( \mathbf{y} \right)~\text{since~}f\left( \mathbf{p} \right) = d$$

content.paragraph: It follows that

But then $d - cf(\textbf{y}) \geq d(1 - c)$ and $cf\left( \textbf{y} \right) \leq d - d(1 - c) = cd$, so $f\left( \textbf{y} \right) \leq d$. On the other hand, $\textbf{y} \in P$, so $f(\textbf{y}) \geq d\text{.}$ It follows that $f(\textbf{y}) = d$ and that $\textbf{y} \in H \cap P$. This contradicts the fact that $\textbf{p}$ is a vertex. So $\textbf{p}$ must be an extreme point. (Note that this part of the proof does not depend on $P$ being a polytope. It holds for any compact convex set.)
(c) $\Rightarrow$ (a) It is clear that any extreme point of $P$ must be a member of $M$.﻿

example.heading: Example 2
example.paragraph: Recall that the profile of a set $S$ is the set of extreme points of $S$. Theorem 14 shows that the profile of a polygon in $\text{ℝ}^{2}$ is the set of vertices. (See Figure 3.) The profile of a closed ball is its boundary. An open set has no extreme points, so its profile is empty. A closed half-space has no extreme points, so its profile is empty.

image.alt: An irregular pentagon, a solid circle, a circle with a dashed-line circumference, and a line with an irregular shape arranged from left to right.

content.paragraph: Exercise 24 asks you to show that a point $\textbf{p}$ in a convex set $S$ is an extreme point of $S$ if and only if, when $\textbf{p}$ is removed from $S$, the remaining points still form a convex set. It follows that if $S^{\ast}$ is any subset of $S$ such that $\text{conv~}S^{\ast}$ is equal to $S$, then $S^{\ast}$ must contain the profile of $S$. The sets in Example 2 show that in general $S^{\ast}$ may have to be larger than the profile of $S$. It is true, however, that when $S$ is compact, we may actually take $S^{\ast}$ to be the profile of $S$, as Theorem 15 will show. Thus every nonempty compact convex set $S$ has an extreme point, and the set of all extreme points is the smallest subset of $S$ whose convex hull is equal to $S$.﻿

note.title: ﻿﻿Theorem ﻿15﻿
note.heading: ﻿﻿Theorem ﻿15﻿
note.paragraph: Let $S$ be a nonempty compact convex set. Then $S$ is the convex hull of its profile (the set of extreme points of $S$).

content.heading: Proof
content.paragraph: The proof is by induction on the dimension of the set $S$.﻿1

One important application of Theorem 15 is the following theorem. It is one of the key theoretical results in the development of linear programming. Linear functionals are continuous, and continuous functions always attain their maximum and minimum on a compact set. The significance of Theorem 16 is that for compact convex sets, the maximum (and minimum) is actually attained at an extreme point of $S$.﻿

content.paragraph: The situation illustrated in Example 3 for $\text{ℝ}^{2}$ also applies in higher dimensions. The maximum value of a linear functional $f$ on a polytope $P$ occurs at the intersection of a supporting hyperplane and $P\text{.}$ This intersection is either a single extreme point of $P\text{,}$ or the convex hull of $2$ or more extreme points of $P\text{.}$ In either case, the intersection is a polytope, and its extreme points form a subset of the extreme points of $P\text{.}$

By definition, a polytope is the convex hull of a finite set of points. This is an explicit representation of the polytope since it identifies points in the set. A polytope may also be represented implicitly as the intersection of a finite number of closed half-spaces. Example 4 illustrates this in $\text{ℝ}^{2}\text{.}$

content.paragraph: The remainder of this section discusses the construction of two basic polytopes in $\text{ℝ}^{3}$, (and higher dimensions). The first appears in linear programming problems, the subject of Chapter 9. Both polytopes provide opportunities to visualize $\text{ℝ}^{4}$ in a remarkable way.
content.heading: Simplex
content.paragraph: A simplex is the convex hull of an affinely independent finite set of vectors. To construct a $k$-dimensional simplex (or $k$-simplex), proceed as follows:

The simplex $S^{1}$ is a line segment. The triangle $S^{2}$ comes from choosing a point $\textbf{v}_{3}$ that is not in the line containing $S^{1}$ and then forming the convex hull with $S^{1}$. (See Figure 6.) The tetrahedron $S^{3}$ is produced by choosing a point $\textbf{v}_{4}$ not in the plane of $S^{2}$ and then forming the convex hull with $S^{2}$.﻿

image.alt: Four Simplex labeled S superscript 0, S superscript 1, S superscript 2, and S superscript 3 are arranged from left to right.

content.paragraph: Before continuing, consider some of the patterns that are appearing. The triangle $S^{2}$ has three edges. Each of these edges is a line segment like $S^{1}$. Where do these three line segments come from? One of them is $S^{1}$. One of them comes by joining the endpoint $\textbf{v}_{2}$ to the new point $\textbf{v}_{3}$. The third comes from joining the other endpoint $\textbf{v}_{1}$ to $\textbf{v}_{3}$. You might say that each endpoint in $S^{1}$ is stretched out into a line segment in $S^{2}$.﻿

The tetrahedron $S^{3}$ in Figure 6 has four triangular faces. One of these is the original triangle $S^{2}$, and the other three come from stretching the edges of $S^{2}$ out to the new point $\textbf{v}_{4}$. Notice too that the vertices of $S^{2}$ get stretched out into edges in $S^{3}$. The other edges in $S^{3}$ come from the edges in $S^{2}$. This suggests how to “visualize” the four-dimensional $S^{4}$.﻿

The construction of $S^{4}$, called a pentatope, involves forming the convex hull of $S^{3}$ with a point $\textbf{v}_{5}$ not in the $\text{3-space}$ of $S^{3}$. A complete picture is impossible, of course, but Figure 7 is suggestive: $S^{4}$ has five vertices, and any four of the vertices determine a facet in the shape of a tetrahedron. For example, the figure emphasizes the facet with vertices $\textbf{v}_{1}$, $\textbf{v}_{2}$, $\textbf{v}_{4}$, and $\textbf{v}_{5}$ and the facet with vertices $\textbf{v}_{2}$, $\textbf{v}_{3}$, $\textbf{v}_{4}$, and $\textbf{v}_{5}$. There are five such facets. Figure 7 identifies all ten edges of $S^{4}$, and these can be used to visualize the ten triangular faces.

is called a $k\text{-dimensional}$ hypercube.

To visualize the construction of $C^{k}$, start with the simple cases. The hypercube $C^{1}$ is the line segment $I_{1}$. If $C^{1}$ is translated by $\textbf{e}_{2}$, the convex hull of its initial and final positions describes a square $C^{2}$. (See Figure 9.) Translating $C^{2}$ by $\textbf{e}_{3}$ creates the cube $C^{3}$. A similar translation of $C^{3}$ by the vector $\textbf{e}_{4}$ yields the $\text{4-dimensional}$ hypercube $C^{4}$.﻿

image.alt: Three figures show the construction of a cube.

content.paragraph: Again, this is hard to visualize, but Figure 10 shows a $\text{2-dimensional}$ projection of $C^{4}$. Each of the edges of $C^{3}$ is stretched into a square facet of $C^{4}$. And each of the square faces of $C^{3}$ is stretched into a cubic facet of $C^{4}$. Figure 11 shows three facets of $C^{4}$. Part (a) highlights the cube that comes from the left square face of $C^{3}$. Part (b) shows the cube that comes from the front square face of $C^{3}$. And part (c) emphasizes the cube that comes from the top square face of $C^{3}$.﻿

content.paragraph: Altogether, the 4-dimensional cube $C^{4}$ has eight cubic facets. Two come from the original and translated images of $C^{3}$, and six come from the square faces of $C^{3}$ that are stretched into cubes. The square 2-dimensional faces of $C^{4}$ come from the square faces of $C^{3}$ and its translate, and the edges of $C^{3}$ that are stretched into squares. Thus there are $2 \times 6 + 12 = 24$ square faces. To count the edges, take $2$ times the number of edges in $C^{3}$ and add the number of vertices in $C^{3}$. This makes $2 \times 12 + 8 = 32$ edges in $C^{4}$. The vertices in $C^{4}$ all come from $C^{3}$ and its translate, so there are $2 \times 8 = 16$ vertices.

One of the truly remarkable results in the study of polytopes is the following formula, first proved by Leonard Euler (1707–1783). It establishes a simple relationship between the number of faces of different dimensions in a polytope. To simplify the statement of the formula, let $f_{k}(P)$ denote the number of $k$-dimensional faces of an $n$-dimensional polytope $P$.﻿3
In particular, when $n = 3,v - e + f = 2$, where $v$, $e$, and $f$ denote the number of vertices, edges, and facets (respectively) of $P$.﻿

(T/F) If $S$ is a nonempty compact convex set and a linear functional attains its maximum at a point $\textbf{p}$, then $\textbf{p}$ is an extreme point of $S$.﻿
(T/F) The $\text{4-dimensional}$ simplex $S^{4}$ has exactly five facets, each of which is a $\text{3-dimensional}$ tetrahedron.
(T/F) A $\text{2-dimensional}$ polytope always has the same number of vertices and edges.
Let $\textbf{v}$ be an element of the convex set $S$. Prove that $\textbf{v}$ is an extreme point of $S$ if and only if the set $\{\textbf{x} \in S:\textbf{x} \neq \textbf{v}\}$ is convex.
If $c \in \text{ℝ}$ and $S$ is a set, define $cS = \left\{ c\textbf{x}:\textbf{x} \in S \right\}$. Let $S$ be a convex set and suppose $c > 0$ and $d > 0$. Prove that $cS + dS = (c + d)S$.﻿
Find an example to show that the convexity of $S$ is necessary in Exercise 25.
If $A$ and $B$ are convex sets, prove that $A + B$ is convex.

A polyhedron $\text{(3-polytope)}$ is called regular if all its facets are congruent regular polygons and all the angles at the vertices are equal. Supply the details in the following proof that there are only five regular polyhedra.

list.item: Suppose that a regular polyhedron has r facets, each of which is a k-sided regular polygon, and that s edges meet at each vertex. Letting v and e denote the numbers of vertices and edges in the polyhedron, explain why kr=2e and sv=2e.﻿
Use Euler’s formula to show that 1s+1k=12+1e.﻿
Find all the integral solutions of the equation in part (b) that satisfy the geometric constraints of the problem. (How small can k and s be?)

statement.paragraph: For your information, the five regular polyhedra are the tetrahedron $(4,~6,~4)$, the cube $(8,~12,~6)$, the octahedron $(6,~12,~8)$, the dodecahedron $(20,~30,~12)$, and the icosahedron $(12,~30,~20)$. (The numbers in parentheses indicate the numbers of vertices, edges, and faces, respectively.)
